British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
<scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐based metacognitive prompting in collaborative inquiry: A comparison across diverse preconception groups
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into collaborative inquiry to provide metacognitive prompting that scaffolds socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Understanding how such GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is taken up through student–GenAI interactions is therefore critical. However, although learner–GenAI interaction processes have been widely examined, little is known about how learners' preconceptions shape their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting. This study examined how groups with different or similar preconceptions about energy forms and conservation differed in their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative inquiry. Participants comprised 14 small groups, including eight groups with different preconceptions (D groups) and six groups with similar preconceptions (S groups). The distribution of learner‐generated inquiries directed to the written metacognitive AI (MAI) was largely comparable across groups. Lag sequential analysis revealed contrasting patterns in how groups evaluated the metacognitive prompts: D groups showed sustained positive or neutral evaluation of the prompts, whereas S groups showed sustained negative evaluation. Process mining further showed that AI query negotiation served as a hub in D groups' collaboration, connecting their conceptual discussions and task coordination. In S groups, by contrast, it formed part of a simpler, linear sequence of querying the AI and processing its responses. This study advances understanding of how preconception diversity shapes the processes and dynamics of human–AI collaboration. The findings show that AI‐mediated regulation varies depending on group‐level knowledge configurations.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Effective collaborative inquiry depends on learners' prior knowledge resources and their regulatory capacity.
                            
                            
                              Preconceptions, as a core component of prior knowledge, shape how learners interpret problems and engage in conceptual discussion.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is designed to externalise metacognitive awareness and scaffold learners' regulatory processes.
                            
                            
                              Regulation unfolds through temporally ordered interaction sequences that reveal underlying regulatory dynamics.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study compares how different preconception groups and similar preconception groups engage with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative scientific inquiry.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting responded to similar types of learner inquiries across groups.
                            
                            
                              GenAI query interaction in different preconception groups appeared more integrated with conceptual and task discussion, whereas in similar preconception groups it followed a more linear, output‐focused path.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting may benefit from incorporating a preliminary classification layer that distinguishes between metacognitive prompts and procedural or informational requests.
                            
                            
                              Teachers may consider preconception diversity when forming groups, as different epistemic configurations appear to give rise to distinct patterns of GenAI‐learner collaboration.
                            
                            
                              Policymakers and designers should recognise that GenAI functions as a co‐regulator within collaborative settings, and its impact depends on how it is interactionally integrated into group interactional trajectories.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    as a team moderator in
                    <scp>CSCL</scp>
                    : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement.
                            
                            
                              While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams.
                            
                            
                              Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding.
                            
                            
                              In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL.
                            
                            
                              Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement.
                            
                            
                              The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs.
                            
                            
                              The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking.
                          
                          
                            Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes.
                          
                          
                            Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting.
                          
                          
                            Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT.
                          
                          
                            Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems.
                          
                          
                            Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning.
                          
                          
                            We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Artificial intelligence and empathetic communication to enhance learning engagement, motivation, and effectiveness
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  With advances in artificial intelligence (AI), textual sentiment analysis has become increasingly popular for extracting word relationships and uncovering hidden emotions. This study applied sentiment analysis to explore students’ emotions during learning because emotions significantly impact motivation and outcomes. Effective teacher-student communication fosters understanding and enhances learning but requires strong empathetic skills to recognize and address students’ emotions. To support this, we developed an AI-assisted learning system integrating KeyMoji, ChatGPT, and Unity that analyzes emotions in real time and provides empathetic responses. The results showed that learning emotions were associated with teacher-student interactions and self-reported academic performance. Students who reported receiving empathetic responses also reported higher engagement and perceived learning outcomes, although these relationships cannot be interpreted as causal given the study design. This study provides preliminary evidence that AI sentiment analysis and empathetic communication are statistically associated with students’ learning emotions, motivation, engagement, and perceived learning outcomes. These findings suggest that AI-generated empathetic feedback supports effective motivational learning processes. The post-test findings indicate that AI-generated empathetic feedback is statistically associated with perceived learning outcomes indirectly through learning emotions and motivation, although these relationships should be interpreted as associational rather than causal, given the post-test single-group research design. Consequently, this study provides a transferable blueprint that advances both affective computing theory and practical digital pedagogy.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Data science for K-12: A design-based research study
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Data science is a field that merges advancements in computer science, statistics, and machine learning. To date, much data science instruction has been through graduate programs or self-directed course offerings. There are therefore fewer opportunities for formal data science education, especially for K-12 educators and learners who have limited exposure to these fields. While some efforts have emerged to introduce data science in pre-college settings, there is little research regarding learning design strategies that support data science for inservice teachers. As such, this project employs a design-based research (DBR) approach to develop accessible and engaging open-access learning resources as a way to reduce barriers to data science instruction across the educational spectrum. Given the gap regarding data science in K-12, our DBR study identifies the following design elements: (a) revised data science content scope, (b) design standardization for interactive learning, (c) reframing data science for case-based learning, (d) artificial intelligence (AI) towards data personalization, and (e) data science coding through goal-based learning. The project also introduces aspects of the curriculum via a teacher professional development, which provides important insights and challenges regarding data science at the middle and high school levels. Implications for learning design, open-educational resources, data science standards, and others are discussed.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Assessing the Impact of Immersive Technologies on Academic Performance, Cognitive Load, Engagement, and Self‐Regulated Learning: A Quasi‐Experimental Study in Kazakhstan
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    
                      The relevance of this study stems from the digital transformation of Kazakhstan's higher education system and the need for pedagogically sound immersive technologies: virtual (
                      VR
                      ) and augmented realities (
                      AR
                      ), capable of improving the quality of education under conditions of limited educational resources.
                    
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This quasi‐experimental study aims to assess the impact of VR/AR technologies on the academic achievement and psychological characteristics (i.e., cognitive load, engagement, and self‐regulated learning strategies) of students pursuing a degree in pedagogy, psychology, engineering, and technology at universities in Kazakhstan.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      This study used a quasi‐experimental design with control and experimental groups and conducted pre‐ and pos
                      t
                      ‐tests to assess the effect of the intervention. The study also used a cognitive load scale and qualitative interviews.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    
                      Results showed a significant increase in academic performance in the VR/AR group (Δ = +22.7%–24.4%; Cohen's
                      d
                       = 1.54–1.78;
                      p
                       < 0.001) as compared to the control group (
                      d
                      ≈0.8–0.9). The overall cognitive load did not increase, but scores for performance (81.5 vs. 73.8;
                      p
                       < 0.001), effort (69.2 vs. 60.7;
                      p
                       < 0.001), and frustration (25.3 vs. 28.9;
                      p
                       = 0.032) were higher. Statistically significant differences were found within the VR/AR group in terms of engagement and self‐regulated learning strategies (
                      p
                       < 0.001). A positive correlation was found between engagement and self‐regulation (
                      r
                       = 0.62), whereas a negative correlation was present between engagement and cognitive load (
                      r
                       = −0.28…−0.31). VR/AR usage had a significant moderating effect (η
                      2
                      ≈0.39–0.42), whereas the moderation effect of university affiliation was insignificant. The proposed conceptual framework has demonstrated its empirical applicability in this study. The results obtained, taking contextual limitations into account, can serve as an empirical basis for the future implementation of virtual and augmented reality solutions.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: When Do Learning Habits Matter? Linking Behavioural Stages to Academic Performance Using Longitudinal Log Data
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Developing effective learning habits—such as studying at regular times—can significantly influence academic performance. While prior research has shown that structured routines benefit learners, most studies rely on self‐reported surveys and provide only a snapshot of behaviour change. Little is known about how learning habits evolve over time or how these shifts affect learning outcomes in technology‐enhanced environments. Addressing this gap is critical for designing personalised, timely support that adapts to learners' behavioural states.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study investigates how learners progress through different stages of learning habit formation and how these stages relate to academic performance over time.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    This study analysed 3 years of daily learning log data from 120 Japanese junior high school students. The data were collected through a school‐wide digital learning environment that integrates a learning management system, a digital e‐book system, and a self‐regulated/directed learning support tool. Grounded in the transtheoretical model of behaviour change, this study extracted learners' monthly habit stages from the log data and examined their relationship with exam performance across nine mathematics assessments.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Academic performance improved significantly as students reached the ‘preparation’ stage, marking a transition from irregular exploratory behaviours to regular weekly study within a single month. However, reaching the ‘maintenance’ stage—the highest stage in the transtheoretical model, representing the culmination of habit‐building through consistent weekly study for at least 4 months—led to performance stabilisation rather than further gains, suggesting a plateau effect once behaviours become automatic. Notably, some learners maintained their academic levels even after regressing to lower habit stages, providing evidence of a residual effect where the cognitive benefits of previously established habits persist despite behavioural fluctuations. This study contributes a novel method for identifying when to offer timely support and suggests how digital learning tools can adapt based on students' habit stages.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Artificial Intelligence in Embodied Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Embodied learning (EL) is an educational approach that posits that cognition develops as learners interact with their environment through physical activity or sensory experiences. Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) supports teaching and learning for both teachers and students, for example through personalised intelligent tutoring systems. However, prior research on EL has focused primarily on students' cognitive and emotional abilities and the integration of body and task, rather than on technological elements, and research on technology‐based embodied learning (TBEL) has centred on immersive technologies such as VR and AR.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aims to explore the relationship between AI technology and EL by analysing (1) the types of AI utilised in EL‐related research (algorithm or model, data modality, AI role), (2) learners' outcomes obtained from AI‐based EL, and (3) the limitations and solutions when applying AI to EL.
                  
                  
                    Method
                    This study is a systematic literature review based on the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and no meta‐analysis was conducted. This study only referenced papers published since 2016 that included both AI technology and EL, were written in English, and dealt with learning processes mediated by physical activity. A study was treated as within scope only where the physical activity was tied to the concept to be learned. Papers were excluded if they did not specify the AI algorithm or model, were not peer‐reviewed, were secondary studies, were not in the field of education, were unavailable in full text, emphasised only simple skill acquisition in physical education or music, or emphasised only simple speaking activities in foreign language learning. Searches were conducted on 16 September 2025 in ACM, ERIC, and Web of Science. Given the diverse types of included studies, risk of bias was assessed using the MMAT2018 tool. Due to the varied nature of the data, a multi‐faceted data synthesis was performed. Co‐occurrences between data modality and AI role, and between AI role and learner outcomes, were visualised using heatmaps. The flow between the three variables was represented using a Sankey diagram. Finally, all frequencies were recalculated after excluding papers appraised as Low or not appraised, to test which patterns depended on weaker evidence.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    A total of 23 papers were reviewed. As multiple data points could be extracted per item, the relative proportion was calculated against the number of coding instances per item. The most frequently used AI algorithm/model in the EL context was deep learning, and the data modality was image data. Where multiple data types were used, it was tagged as multimodal, accounting for 34.8%. Analysis and evaluation roles were most frequently extracted, and cognitive outcomes were reported most often. Key limitations identified included restricted participant numbers due to research design and studies conducted in controlled environments. Among papers appraised as High, the most frequent pathways ran from multimodal data to recognition and detection and from sensor data to analysis and evaluation, and cognitive outcomes were the most frequently reported. When papers appraised as Low or not appraised were set aside, the concentration of AI in analytical roles persisted, whereas the evidence for AI as an interactive or generative participant weakened.
                  
                  
                    Discussion
                    This review describes reported patterns rather than pooled effect estimates, as no meta‐analysis was conducted. Exclusion of grey literature may introduce publication bias. Furthermore, the potential risk of selection bias exists as literature was collected based on inclusion/exclusion criteria. This study is significant in that it identified how AI is utilised within the EL context and the learner outcomes reported alongside it, particularly as the scope of AIED broadens.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants (
                    n
                    = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Socratic, Artifact-Gated Generative AI Scaffolding in a 6E Inquiry Unit: A Clustered Quasi-Experiment in Elementary Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer (
                    B

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Prompting to Scaffolding: Divergent Human–AI Interaction Pathways of Pre-Service Teachers in Multi-Agent Micro-Teaching Simulation (MAMS)
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Traditional micro-teaching offers limited opportunities for pre-service teachers to rehearse classroom contingencies in repeatable, standardized ways. This study developed a multi-agent micro-teaching simulation (MAMS), informed by professional noticing, to expand practice-based learning opportunities for pre-service mathematics teachers (PSTs). MAMS integrates differentiated virtual students, standardized challenge events, and Dean Agent prompts to create comparable classroom contingencies. Sixty-four PSTs completed two simulated micro-teaching sessions and were analytically classified into higher and lower baseline mathematics pedagogical content knowledge (MPCK) profiles. Outcomes included teacher self-efficacy, MPCK performance, and Community of Inquiry presence; interaction logs were analyzed using event-anchored lag sequential analysis. Under the standardized MAMS condition, outcome analyses showed observed pre–post changes and modest baseline-adjusted profile differences. The higher baseline MPCK profile showed stronger MPCK response-strategy performance and higher Teaching Presence; Social and Cognitive Presence showed no reliable profile differences. Log analyses revealed divergent feedback-to-action pathways: higher baseline MPCK PSTs more often moved from Dean Agent prompts to diagnostic questioning and scaffolding, followed by substantive student responses, whereas lower baseline MPCK PSTs more often shifted to direct instruction or process regulation, followed by continued low participation. These findings suggest a need for prior-knowledge-responsive scaffolding in AI-supported teacher education.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: From Local to Global: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Validation of the SAGAI Scale for Measuring Student Attitudes Toward Generative AI
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming an increasingly visible component of higher education, raising the need for theoretically grounded instruments that can capture how students perceive and engage with these technologies. This study aims to adapt the Scale for Attitudes toward Generative Artificial Intelligence (SAGAI), originally developed in Turkish, into English and to examine its psychometric properties within a different linguistic context. The study was conducted with 350 higher education students enrolled at a UK-based open and distance learning institution. A systematic cross-cultural adaptation process was followed, including translation, back-translation, expert review, and pilot testing. Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to examine the structural validity of the scale. The findings supported a four-factor structure—usefulness, anxiety, expectancy, and competency—consistent with the original model, with acceptable to strong model fit indices after minor modifications, resulting in a 22-item version. Reliability analyses indicated high internal consistency across all dimensions. Comparative analyses examined differences between the Turkish and English samples at both total and dimensional levels. Turkish participants reported higher levels of usefulness, expectancy, and anxiety, whereas English participants demonstrated higher perceived competency. Additional analyses within the UK sample indicated that prior experience with GenAI was strongly associated with attitudinal differences, pointing to the role of usage in shaping how these technologies are evaluated. The findings indicate that the underlying structure of attitudes toward GenAI remains stable across linguistic contexts, while the intensity and balance of these dimensions vary depending on contextual and experiential factors. The coexistence of positive expectations and concerns suggests that student attitudes toward GenAI are inherently multidimensional rather than uniformly positive or negative. The study provides evidence that SAGAI is a valid and reliable instrument for use in English-speaking contexts and offers a structured framework for examining student attitudes toward GenAI in cross-cultural research. The results also underline the importance of considering both context and experience when interpreting how students engage with emerging technologies.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: What counts as digital play? Irish early childhood educators’ beliefs and practice tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly embedded in young children’s lives, yet uncertainty remains regarding their role in early childhood education and care (ECEC). This study explores Irish early years educators’ beliefs and perceptions concerning digital play, employing Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological framework to examine how policy, parental expectations and professional identity interact to shape children’s learning opportunities. Semi-structured interviews with 10 educators identified five themes: developmentalist beliefs prioritising ‘natural’ play, cautious openness to digital tools, professional identity and ethical tensions, perceptions of children and families and concerns about policy directives. Findings reveal a persistent policy–practice gap, where limited professional development and unclear guidance leave educators uncertain about how to define and implement quality digital play. The study emphasises that educators’ attitudes are closely associated with the extent and quality of children’s digital engagement, highlighting the need for sustained professional development and strengthened mesosystemic communication across home, school and policy contexts. Implications include the creation of context-sensitive frameworks that integrate digital and traditional play while supporting children’s holistic development. This study demonstrates that educators’ definitions of digital play are shaped by the interaction of professional identity, policy ambiguity, family expectations and resource conditions, offering new insight into the conditions that constrain digital play in Irish early years settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Teachers’ professional learning and development experiences in Chinese kindergartens: Opportunities and tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Professional learning and development (PLD) activities for Chinese kindergarten teachers have introduced imported knowledge to promote teaching and learning. Much PLD provision is led by leaders and experts rather than teachers. To understand the educational beliefs and power differences that surface among teachers, leaders and experts during PLD sessions and how teachers navigate this complex terrain, this paper presents a post-intentional phenomenological study involving seven participants from two Chinese early childhood settings. Data collection included semi-structured interviews, observations of PLD meetings and videos of teachers’ implementation of PLD ideas. Educational policies, PLD materials, and the researcher’s reflexive journal were also used for analysis. Analysis involved a line-by-line reading process where theoretical concepts, data and researcher reflexivity interacted. The findings reveal that teachers experienced tensions in relation to formal PLD sessions. These tensions stemmed from established values and hierarchical constraints that limited their joint reflection and actions. Our analysis, framed by the concepts of relational agency and in-between spaces, shows how teachers navigated these tensions. Despite these constraints, the teachers responded by creating opportunities for collaborative learning. They sought out informal situations where they had the flexibility to develop shared knowledge. We argue that Chinese teachers’ PLD can occur within and across such tensions and opportunities. These informal situations empowered teachers to enact relational agency by aligning their expertise to make PLD decisions. This process eased tensions and created space for collaborative learning. The study concludes that valuing these informal, teacher-initiated spaces is crucial for moving beyond top-down knowledge transmission and fostering sustainable professional growth in hierarchical educational contexts. Ultimately, by empowering teachers as collaborative and adaptable professionals, this model of PLD offers new insights into enhancing the professional environments that shape teaching practice and young children’s learning.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Parent–school mobile communication in preschool: A qualitative study in Mexico
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: School-family communication in early childhood is increasingly mediated by mobile applications, yet important questions remain about what counts as high-quality content, how schools allocate topics between digital and face-to-face channels, and what costs these practices impose on teachers. This qualitative study examines how a mobile application shapes day-to-day parent-school communication in a Mexican preschool. Semi-structured interviews with four teachers and three mothers, combined with field observation, were thematically analyzed. The app supported timely and consistent exchanges about classroom life. Families valued brief, concrete descriptions of children’s socio-emotional participation, peer interactions, and strategies practiced, along with simple suggestions for follow-up at home. However, participants identified a depth gap when messages focused mainly on logistics, and teachers reported a workload tension between the burden of exhaustive daily reporting and the sense of security it provides to parents. A hybrid model of communication was preferred: routine updates and nonurgent questions were handled in the app, while complex, evaluative, or sensitive topics were addressed in planned one-to-one meetings. Reported short-term gains were primarily psychosocial, including higher trust and a closer working relationship between teachers and families. Findings support a shift from tool adoption to the quality of communicative practice in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Promoting social skills and friendships in early childhood education: A case study of four children’s trajectories to inclusion
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper reports on the changes reported on the social relations and skills of four children after the implementation of ProFriend (Promoting Friendship) in an early childhood education (ECE) setting. ProFriend is a programme developed considering the inclusive ECE principles by targeting all children’s access and participation and looking beyond imposed labels. The data of the study included friendship nominations, observations, children’s drawings, teachers’ interviews and research diary. The findings shed light on four children’s trajectories who faced challenges in forming friendships and whose individual characteristics (speech and language impairments and socio-emotional difficulties) were seen by teachers as barriers to their social development. The discussion focuses on how children’s exclusion can be minimised by enriching ECE curricula with some elements guiding teachers on how to approach the development of social skills and friendships in a meaningful and inclusive way.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The impact of active transitions on preschool students’ self-regulation
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood education plays a pivotal role in fostering the holistic development of young learners through age-appropriate activities and interactions that support physical, social, emotional and cognitive growth. This study explored the relationship between active transitions in an early childhood education classroom and observable behaviour indicators of self-regulation in preschoolers, with a specific focus on the integration of yoga during transitional times. The objective was to investigate the impact of incorporating yoga on student self-regulation during large group literacy, as perceived by the preschool teacher. The research employed a collaborative action research design, engaging a preschool teacher in a reflective and systematic approach to improve classroom practices. Findings indicated that the integration of yoga, when including both challenging and sedentary poses, was associated with reductions in teacher-observed off-task behaviour during large group literacy, suggesting a possible positive influence on behaviour self-regulation. Results indicated that active transitions may support overall classroom management, increased instructional time and contributed to a comprehensive understanding of the effects of physical activity on young learners.

keyword_papers.title: ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education
keyword_papers.abstract: Large language models represent a significant advancement in the field of AI. The underlying technology is key to further innovations and, despite critical views and even bans within communities and regions, large language models are here to stay. This position paper presents the potential benefits and challenges of educational applications of large language models, from student and teacher perspectives. We briefly discuss the current state of large language models and their applications. We then highlight how these models can be used to create educational content, improve student engagement and interaction, and personalize learning experiences. With regard to challenges, we argue that large language models in education require teachers and learners to develop sets of competencies and literacies necessary to both understand the technology as well as their limitations and unexpected brittleness of such systems. In addition, a clear strategy within educational systems and a clear pedagogical approach with a strong focus on critical thinking and strategies for fact checking are required to integrate and take full advantage of large language models in learning settings and teaching curricula. Other challenges such as the potential bias in the output, the need for continuous human oversight, and the potential for misuse are not unique to the application of AI in education. But we believe that, if handled sensibly, these challenges can offer insights and opportunities in education scenarios to acquaint students early on with potential societal biases, criticalities, and risks of AI applications. We conclude with recommendations for how to address these challenges and ensure that such models are used in a responsible and ethical manner in education.

keyword_papers.title: Student perceptions of ChatGPT: benefits, costs, and attitudinal differences between users and non-users toward AI integration in higher education
keyword_papers.abstract: Today, there is no doubt that Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents both opportunities and challenges in higher education. This study examines three key areas: (1) students’ use of ChatGPT, (2) their perceptions of its benefits and costs, and (3) the differences in attitudes toward AI integration in higher education between ChatGPT users and non-users. A sample of 737 undergraduate students at a Spanish university answered an online survey. The quantitative analysis revealed a high prevalence of ChatGPT use for academic and personal purposes, with students identifying its 24/7 accessibility as a major advantage, along with the time-saving benefits it offers. However, concerns were raised about potential costs, including the devaluation of university education when students rely on ChatGPT to complete assignments. Results indicate significant differences between ChatGPT users and non-users: users generally support AI integration in higher education, particularly in teaching methods, while non-users often oppose its integration, advocating for measures such as banning AI in universities. Our study provides valuable insights into student perspectives on the integration of ChatGPT in higher education, emphasizing the contrasting viewpoints of users and non-users. The findings underline the need for universities to actively involve students in shaping policies on artificial intelligence while offering targeted training to promote its responsible and ethical use. Furthermore, universities should support educators in adapting their teaching methodologies to the digital era by incorporating innovative strategies that enhance both teaching and learning.
keyword_papers.venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

keyword_papers.title: Assessing Student Readiness and Perceptions of ChatGPT in Learning: A Case Study in Indonesian Higher Education
keyword_papers.abstract:
Aim/Purpose: This study investigates the readiness of higher education students in Indonesia to use ChatGPT for learning and explores its perceived benefits in academic settings. The research aims to identify challenges and opportunities in integrating generative AI into education.

Background: As a rapidly evolving AI technology, ChatGPT presents both opportunities and challenges in higher education. While it offers convenience and personalized support, concerns regarding ethical use, academic integrity, and student dependency remain. Understanding student readiness and attitudes toward ChatGPT is essential for effective and responsible implementation in learning environments. 

Methodology: This study employs a mixed-methods convergent parallel design, collecting both quantitative and qualitative data simultaneously but analyzing them separately. A total of 373 students from diverse universities and disciplines in Indonesia participated. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Rasch measurement model and Winsteps software, while qualitative responses were transcribed and examined through summative content analysis using Quirkos 2.5.3 software. Participants were selected through a purposive sampling approach to ensure a representative distribution across institutions and fields of study.

Contribution: This study contributes to the growing discourse on AI in education by offering clear, data-driven insights into Indonesian students’ readiness and perceptions of ChatGPT. It reveals that students across diverse regions view ChatGPT as a helpful academic tool, particularly for clarifying complex concepts, reducing stress, and supporting independent learning. These findings provide actionable guidance for educators and policymakers, highlighting the urgent need for AI literacy programs and ethical use policies. The study lays a strong empirical foundation for larger-scale, longitudinal research on AI integration in higher education by presenting these concrete patterns.

Findings: The findings indicate a generally high level of student readiness to use ChatGPT in learning contexts. Students perceive ChatGPT as a valuable tool for completing assignments, clarifying complex concepts, and reducing academic stress. However, concerns were also raised regarding its potential impact on critical thinking skills and the need for clear ethical guidelines. These findings provide preliminary evidence that can support the development of institutional strategies and future research directions.

Recommendations for Practitioners: For educators and institutions, it is crucial to develop structured policies and ethical guidelines for ChatGPT use in academic contexts. Assignments should be designed to promote higher-order thinking skills, such as creativity and problem-solving, rather than mere fact recall. Additionally, AI literacy training should be incorporated into curricula to help students critically evaluate AI-generated content.

Recommendation for Researchers: For researchers, future studies should explore the readiness of educators to integrate ChatGPT into teaching and assess its long-term impact on student learning outcomes, including critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Investigating how ChatGPT can be effectively embedded within existing learning management systems could further enhance its educational potential.

Impact on Society: By identifying both the benefits and challenges of ChatGPT in higher education, this study informs policies and best practices for AI adoption in academia. Addressing issues of digital equity, ethical concerns, and pedagogical strategies can help create a more balanced and effective AI-assisted learning environment, ultimately improving the quality of education and teaching methodologies.

Future Research: Further research should investigate how ChatGPT influences long-term student engagement, skill development, and academic performance. Studies should also examine institutional readiness, faculty perspectives, and AI’s role in fostering more interactive and adaptive learning experiences.

keyword_papers.title: Empowering student self-regulated learning and science education through ChatGPT: A pioneering pilot study
keyword_papers.abstract:
In recent years, AI technologies have been developed to promote students' self‐regulated learning (SRL) and proactive learning in digital learning environments. This paper discusses a comparative study between generative AI‐based (SRLbot) and rule‐based AI chatbots (Nemobot) in a 3‐week science learning experience with 74 Secondary 4 students in Hong Kong. The experimental group used SRLbot to maintain a regular study habit and facilitate their SRL, while the control group utilized rule‐based AI chatbots. Results showed that SRLbot effectively enhanced students' science knowledge, behavioural engagement and motivation. Quantile regression analysis indicated that the number of interactions significantly predicted variations in SRL. Students appreciated the personalized recommendations and flexibility of SRLbot, which adjusted responses based on their specific learning and SRL scenarios. The ChatGPT‐enhanced instructional design reduced learning anxiety and promoted learning performance, motivation and sustained learning habits. Students' feedback on learning challenges, psychological support and self‐regulation behaviours provided insights into their progress and experience with this technology. SRLbot's adaptability and personalized approach distinguished it from rule‐based chatbots. The findings offer valuable evidence for AI developers and educators to consider generative AI settings and chatbot design, facilitating greater success in online science learning.
What is already known about this topic

AI technologies have been used to support student self‐regulated learning (SRL) across subjects.
SRL has been identified as an important aspect of student learning that can be developed through technological support.
Generative AI technologies like ChatGPT have shown potential for enhancing student learning by providing personalized guidance and feedback.
What this paper adds

This paper reports on a case study that specifically examines the effectiveness of ChatGPT in promoting SRL among secondary students.
The study provides evidence that ChatGPT can enhance students' science knowledge, motivation and SRL compared to a rule‐based AI chatbot.
The study offers insights into how ChatGPT can be used as a tool to facilitate SRL and promote sustained learning habits.
Implications for practice and/or policy

The findings of this study suggest that educators should consider the potential of ChatGPT and other generative AI technologies to support student learning and SRL.
Educators and students should be aware of the limitations of AI technologies and ensure that they are used appropriately to generate desired responses.
It is also important to equip teachers and students with AI competencies to enable them to use AI for learning and teaching.

keyword_papers.title: ChatGPT Early Adoption in Higher Education: Variation in Student Usage, Instructional Support, and Educational Equity
keyword_papers.abstract: This study examines the early adoption of ChatGPT in late 2022 and early 2023 by identifying variation in student awareness, academic use, and perceived instructional support for the technology at a diverse U.S. public research university. Specifically, we investigate (a) how individual awareness and academic use of ChatGPT vary by student characteristics and field of study, (b) how instructor encouragement or discouragement varies across courses and student demographics, and (c) how academic use patterns differ between science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and non-STEM fields. Data from 938 undergraduates, merged with administrative records, revealed disparities in ChatGPT awareness and use, with underrepresented minority, first-generation, and international students less likely to know about or use the tool academically. Course-level analysis highlighted that instructor encouragement is more prevalent in STEM fields and upper-division courses but decreases in classes with higher underrepresented minority representation. Open-ended responses showed distinct patterns of ChatGPT use, with STEM students favoring conceptual assistance and coding and non-STEM students engaging in writing and instructor-assigned activities. These findings underscore early inequities in access and use of emerging educational technologies and call for institutional strategies to promote equitable awareness and skill development aligned with academic and professional goals.

keyword_papers.title: The impact of educational robot R1 on the development of emotional intelligence in preschool-aged children
keyword_papers.abstract: The study investigates the impact of the educational robot R1 on the development of emotional intelligence in preschool-aged children. Employing a convergent mixed methods design with a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test structure and elements of an embedded case study, the research was conducted in a kindergarten in Athens with 21 children aged 4 to 6 years, including both typically and atypically developing children. Quantitative data were collected through rating rubrics, evaluation sheets, and worksheets, while qualitative insights were obtained via semi-structured interviews and observation. The findings revealed a significant increase in children's emotional intelligence scores across four domains—recognition of emotions, expression of emotions, regulation of emotions, and social skills—following the interventions. Children demonstrated enhanced emotional vocabulary, self-awareness, management of emotions, and collaborative behaviors. The robot served as a socially engaging tool, promoting both affective learning and peer interaction. These results support the integration of educational robotics into early childhood education to foster emotional and social development in inclusive and diverse classroom environments.

keyword_papers.title: Object Recognition-Based Second Language Learning Educational Robot System for Chinese Preschool Children
keyword_papers.abstract: Research in psychology, pedagogy, and physiology has shown that learning a second language will be a great benefit to preschool children. Compared with adults, children have more advantages in learning, such as better pronunciation and intonation. However, because of children’s inattention, the effects of the second language education in many preschools are not ideal in China. To make children learn the second language effectively, it should be integrated into their daily lives and in line with their interests. In this paper, an educational robot system with object recognition technology is introduced, which aims to provide innovative second language learning services for preschool children in China. The proposed system combines object recognition and projection with English teaching and makes objects in daily life more interesting with projected animation to attract children’s attention. On the projection screen, children can interact with a robot by touch or movement and can easily trigger more interactive effects. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed system, we conducted an experiment, and the results showed that the system can improve the language learning efficiency for the Chinese preschool children by interacting with objects under proper guidance.

keyword_papers.title: The Impact of Educational Robotics on the Executive Functions of Preschool Children
keyword_papers.abstract: This quasi-experimental study examines the impact of an educational robotics program on the development of executive functions (EF) in preschool children in Morocco. Throughout the school year, 84 pupils from two schools in Rabat and Salé participated in a progressive program that combined unplugged activities with the exploration of the Bee-Bot robot. Five key dimensions (planning, working memory, cognitive flexibility, problem-solving, and collaboration) were assessed using a 22-indicator grid to measure the children’s progress in these areas. Data collection occurred over a seven-day period. Statistical analysis highlighted significant inter-dimensional correlations (0.533 ≤ r ≤ 0.931, p < 0.001), indicating a strong interdependence between the skills developed and higher mean scores for the early stages of the program (notably spatial planning and getting to grips with the Bee-Bot). Conversely, problem-solving and collaboration, although more demanding, appeared to be closely linked (r = 0.931), suggesting that the consolidation of individual problem-solving skills creates favorable conditions for mutual aid and collective work. These results confirm that the gradual, supervised integration of educational robotics can enhance executive functions in early childhood by engaging working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility through structured, interactive activities. This study thus contributes to a better understanding of the potential of educational robotics in a non-Western context and lays the groundwork for future longitudinal and comparative research exploring how cultural and pedagogical factors influence early childhood learning outcomes.

keyword_papers.title: The Impact of AI-based Smart Robot Education on the Sociality of Preschool Children Mediated by Creative Problem-solving and Linguistic Expression
keyword_papers.abstract: This research investigates the educational effectiveness of a smart robot program integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the sociality of preschool children, particularly focusing on the mediating roles of creative problem-solving and linguistic expression. As the Fourth Industrial Revolution reshapes the educational landscape, AI-driven media have emerged as a ‘Social catalyst’ that significantly accelerates early childhood development. This study employed a quantitative experimental design involving a large-scale sample of 300 preschool children (150 boys and 150 girls) aged 5 to 6 years from various kindergartens in Sejong City. The participants were divided into an experimental group (n=150) that engaged in a 12-week AI-based smart robot program and a control group (n=150) that followed a traditional curriculum. Data were collected through the Social Skills Rating System (SSRS), Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT), and standardized linguistic assessments. The results demonstrate that the AI voice-interactive robot program significantly augmented children's sociality scores across all sub-factors. Notably, mediation analysis confirmed that linguistic expression acted as a more potent mediator (b =.45, p <.001) compared to creative problem-solving (b =.38, p <.01), identifying vocal interaction as the primary driver of social development. Statistical analysis further revealed that these variables partially mediated the relationship between AI interaction and sociality. Furthermore, while both genders showed significant improvement, girls demonstrated higher engagement in emotional rapport via voice interaction, whereas boys exhibited greater gains in task-oriented problem-solving. This study concludes that pedagogically sound AI voice-interactive tools are effective for fostering social development in young learners. These findings provide practical implications for educators and media content developers to design immersive and interactive AI educational environments.

keyword_papers.title: Integrating social learning and experiential learning theories: a novel augmented reality approach to enhancing social skills in early childhood education
keyword_papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines the effectiveness of augmented reality (AR)-based learning in enhancing early childhood social skills through the integration of social learning theory and experiential learning theory. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test control group design, the research involved 30 children aged 5–6 years at Telkom Kindergarten, Makassar, Indonesia. The experimental group (n = 15) participated in AR-based storytelling activities designed to foster social skills, while the control group (n = 15) engaged in conventional learning activities. Statistical analysis showed that the AR intervention produced significantly greater effectiveness (N-Gain = 0.73) compared to conventional methods (N-Gain = 0.03). The experimental group demonstrated about 49% improvement across all social skills components, including teamwork, adjustment, interaction, self-control, empathy, discipline, and respect for others. The novelty of this research lies in combining observational learning with direct experiential engagement through AR, creating an effective environment for social skills development that surpasses single-framework approaches. These findings provide strong evidence that well-designed AR-based learning can transform early childhood education by addressing multiple aspects of social competence. The study highlights the potential of emerging technologies to support holistic child development when grounded in comprehensive theoretical foundations and implemented with child-centered pedagogical practices.

keyword_papers.title: The impact of augmented reality-assisted structured learning on environmental education for preschool children
keyword_papers.abstract: Environmental education in preschool plays a crucial role in achieving several of the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by fostering young children’s early awareness, sustainable habits, and eco-conscious attitudes. However, implementing this education through traditional teaching methods is challenging due to the complexity of abstract concepts and a lack of the interactivity and engagement needed to meet the diverse needs of preschool children. This study proposed an Augmented Reality Mobile Game-Based Learning (ARM-GBL) approach with physical play to enhance preschool environmental education based on Mayer’s Selection-Organization-Integration (SOI) model. To examine the impact of ARM-GBL on preschool children’s socio-emotional collaboration and learning performance, a true experimental design was employed. Participants were randomly assigned to two groups: 13 in the ARM-GBL group and 14 in the Digital Game Based Learning (DGBL) group. Results showed that ARM-GBL significantly enhanced socio-emotional skills, such as teamwork and empathy, through collaborative and interactive loose parts play. Furthermore, the ARM-GBL group outperformed the DGBL group in learning performance, achieving better retention of environmental concepts and improved accuracy in tasks such as waste sorting. This research highlights the transformative potential of ARM-GBL by integrating AR technology with structured instructional frameworks and physical play. ARM-GBL effectively addresses both cognitive and socio-emotional developmental needs, offering an engaging and impactful approach to environmental education for preschool children.

keyword_papers.title: Exploring The Future of Early Childhood Education : Research Trends and Implementation of Augmented Reality
keyword_papers.abstract: This study aims to examine the research trends and implementation of Augmented Reality (AR) technology in improving various aspects of child development, the challenges of its implementation, and the direction of future research in the context of digital education for early childhood. This study uses the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) method, with a bibliometric mapping approach and content analysis. A total of 17 articles were selected from the Scopus and DOAJ database in the period 2019–2024 for further analysis. The research findings show that the use of AR significantly enhances the learning experience to be more interactive, contextual, and enjoyable for children. In addition, AR has proven effective in conveying abstract concepts visually and helping to reinforce practical values such as financial responsibility from an early age. However, challenges such as limited infrastructure, access to technology, uneven teacher training, and excessive dependence on technology are major obstacles to the widespread implementation of AR. The implications of this study highlight the importance of increasing technological support in educational institutions, developing AR applications that are aligned with the curriculum, and continuous teacher training. Thus, AR has great potential as an innovative medium in early childhood education, as long as it is balanced with the right implementation strategy.

keyword_papers.title: Augmented Reality in Biology Education: A Literature Review
keyword_papers.abstract: This systematic review summarises the latest research on the use of augmented reality (AR) in biology education at primary, secondary and tertiary levels. Searching Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar, we found 40 empirical studies published up until early 2024. For each study, we analysed biological content, technical features, learning practices and pedagogical impact. AR is most used in human anatomy, particularly in the circulatory and respiratory systems, but also in genetics, cell biology, virology, botany, ecology and molecular processes. Mobile devices dominate as a mediation platform, with marker-based tracking and either commercial apps or self-developed Unity/Vuforia solutions. Almost all studies embed AR in constructivist or inquiry-based pedagogies, and report improved motivation, engagement and conceptual understanding. Nevertheless, reporting on the technical details is inconsistent and the long-term effects are not yet sufficiently researched. AR should therefore be viewed as a pedagogical tool rather than a technological goal that requires careful instructional design and equitable access to ensure meaningful and sustainable learning.

keyword_papers.title: Towards Sustainable Education with the Use of Mobile Augmented Reality in Early Childhood and Primary Education: A Systematic Mapping
keyword_papers.abstract: Over the years, educational institutions have faced significant difficulties in the teaching process at all educational levels, due to lack of motivation, concentration, attention, and confidence, among other aspects. In this sense, information and communication technologies can be the answer to transform educational models. One of the most promising and accessible technologies in recent years is mobile augmented reality (MAR), which allows students to visualize content through a mobile device combining the real environment with a virtual environment, providing an interactive and digital vision of the physical world in real time. The appropriate use of digital technologies in early childhood and primary education can promote socialization, comprehension, learning, language development, attention, and other educational benefits. However, due to the novelty of this technology, there is limited research and a gap in the literature on the use of MAR at these educational levels. This research work, through systematic mapping, aims to give an overview of how AR and mobile devices have been used in the last decade, which academic areas have benefited from the use of this innovative academic approach, and the main benefits and problems of using this technology in early and primary education. The findings are encouraging and show that AR technology, together with mobile devices, can be used to support the teaching of science, mathematics, reading, language, geography, etc.
